newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Pressure increases on Sweden to join ERM.
newsitem.headline: Pressure increases on Sweden to join ERM.

text.p: European central banks were clearly stepping up pressure on Sweden to join Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) but the decision remains a political one, economists said on Thursday.

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer on Thursday said a link to ERM was essential before joining Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), pushing aside the Swedish government's arguments that such a link is not necessary.
His comments came just days after European Monetary Institute president, Alexandre Lamfalussy, said a country should be linked to ERM for two years before joining EMU.

But economists said the interpretation of EMU membership criteria as laid out in the Maastricht Treaty remained open - and ultimately any move to link the crown to ERM was a political decision for the Swedish government.
"It is still open to interpretation," economist Katharine Hoyland of JP Morgan told Reuters. "Nothing has been laid in stone yet."
Sweden argues that ERM membership is not a prerequisite for joining the EMU that is due to come into force on January 1, 1999, saying currency stability is sufficient.
"It is clear that you need a stable currency for two years but do you really need to be a member of the ERM mechanism?" said economist Knut Hallberg from Swedbank.
"Clearly other central banks are trying to push Sweden towards ERM but what is important is what happens politically.
"I am not sure that the same pressure is coming from other prime ministers as I think they understand Sweden has political problems particularly in the (ruling) Social Democrat Party."
Polls have found Sweden is one of the most reluctant countries to join the EMU. A recent survey showed 36 percent of Swedes thought joining the EU in 1995 was the wrong move.
Hoyland said such domestic pressures politically were one reason to keep Sweden out of the ERM.
But she also said the fluctuations of the crown since 1992 did not lay the path for ERM links.
"It is very hard to see if the current level now is a level that can be sustained," Hoyland said.

A Stockholm-based economist, who requested anonymity, said Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, was well aware of the need for stability in the crown and this was why it has now started to intervene in the market as foreshadowed last month.
Twice this week the central bank was rumoured to be active in the market.
"The Riksbank has been very much pro-ERM, much more so than the government, but this could be because it is more in contact with other central banks and feeling the pressure," he said.
He said there was still plenty of room for interpretation of the criteria in the Maastricht Treaty.
"If Sweden fulfils all other criteria and says clearly it wants to join the EMU in 1999, I think it is very unlikely that not being a member of ERM will stop this," he said.
"I think the Riksbank will continue to intervene more frequently now to ensure a stable level in the crown, not a set level but to avoid any too rapid changes."
